title: Making a Magazine: Only the Truly Cool Can Make It Cool
excerpt: What print will become is being decided by a growing variety of players. This is a better era for it, not a worse one.
body:
What print will become is being decided by a growing variety of players. This is a better era for it, not a worse one.

Over the past couple of days, a WeChat article titled "The World's Best Magazine Has Shut Down" passed 100,000 views. Yet many of the people who clicked on it may never have heard of the magazine in question, COLORS.

True, COLORS has faded. Plenty of arty young people once adored it. It was never a giant of the magazine world, but it dared to do what it meant to do. In today's fashionable phrase, it had wild ideas and a cool attitude.

That said, we checked: COLORS magazine's Facebook page, its Twitter account and its official website, Colorsmagazine.com, carry no announcement that it has closed. Chen Jiaojiao, editor-in-chief of *New Vision*, who has worked with COLORS, also denied the rumor in her WeChat Moments. Passing on a text message from Mrs. Benetton, she said COLORS had not shut down at all; it had just produced a publication for its 25th anniversary.

Many people probably know that the magazine hailed as the "best" is backed not by a media group but by the clothing brand Benetton, though you may well not know Benetton. To make an imperfect comparison, it was a bit like the early Baleno, only much more expensive. It specialized in saturated solid colors, which, mixed and matched, looked young and bold at the time.

Benetton was founded in Italy in 1965. It first sold mainly hand-knitted sweaters, then gradually moved into casual wear. In China it once had counters in many department stores, but once the first "fast fashion" brands such as Baleno and Esprit took off, it declined fast. You may still spot it in one or two places, but young people probably know little about it.

The brand has, in fact, always been bold. The ad of heads of state kissing that shocked the world came from Benetton. With the brand's backing, Oliviero Toscani, Tibor Kalman and Karrie Jacobs (more on who they are later) founded the magazine, and the editorial office moved from New York, where the three had lived, to Rome, where the company is based.

![Benetton billboard showing Kim Il-sung and South Korean President Lee Myung-bak kissing](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703152013vyHnMq4GJtOALzs1.jpg-w600)In Benetton's 2013 outdoor ads, Kim Il-sung and then South Korean President Lee Myung-bak share a kiss. The campaign paired six couples in all, including Obama and Venezuela's Chávez, and German Chancellor Merkel and French President Sarkozy. The idea came from the famous Berlin Wall mural of Soviet leader Brezhnev kissing East Germany's Erich Honecker.

The rumor of its closure most likely started because the new 2015 issue never arrived as expected. COLORS comes out irregularly, and amid so much information, being forgotten is normal. Of course, we can't say how its quality has changed lately. But at least it isn't dead.

Many people have asked a simple question: why would a clothing company run a magazine? Is Benetton an oddity?

![Cover of COLORS issue 90, on football](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703152014IKNna7HFPC2keTov.jpg-w600)COLORS issue 90 uses football to look at the globalization of entertainment

The answer is simple: because it's cool.

One common explanation goes like this. Every company gives its marketing department a large budget, spent either on advertising or on celebrity endorsers. For the same money, a magazine doesn't cost much more. And a magazine has an obvious advantage: it comes with its own reach, its own voice and everything it takes to look cool. As long as you find the right people, why not?

COLORS launched in 1991. In 1993, issue 4 devoted the whole magazine to race; issue 7 took up AIDS; issue 41 changed the cover typeface and, with help from the UN refugee agency (UNHCR), covered refugees. In 2005, having just moved its office from Rome to New York, COLORS made "freedom of speech" the theme of its new issue and put graffiti by Tsang Tsou-choi, the self-styled "King of Kowloon", on the cover. COLORS has also used a full sheet of stickers as a cover, and gave away a yellow card with an issue on football. That gives you a sense of the "avant-garde" reputation people talk about.

Over the magazine's 20-plus years, Benetton's ads appeared in a similar style, and the two borrowed material from each other. The cover of COLORS' first issue was a photograph by Oliviero Toscani, which also ran in Benetton's print ads.

From the 1990s on, Benetton's ads boldly used images tied to sensitive subjects such as condoms, the electric chair and race, and took on the relationship between people and nature and unemployment. These themes ran in the same vein as the magazine.

![Benetton ad using the same photograph as the first COLORS cover](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703152015AgQihk0mrbj3PwlK.jpg-w600)A Benetton ad that uses the same photograph as the first issue's cover

![Covers of COLORS issues 51 to 66](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703152015hXgQJ02S18fDBTjo.jpg-w600)Covers of COLORS issues 51 to 66

"It champions diversity, so it can reach more people," said Cosimo Bizzarri, a senior editor at COLORS. Andrew Losowsky of Stanford University put it this way: "The magazine doesn't talk about things we don't know. It just makes new connections between everyday things."

Benetton has said it would never alter the magazine's content, but readers can still sense, indirectly, the brand values Benetton wants to promote.

Many companies have used magazines to look cool (and, of course, to inspire generation after generation of readers). Some people are still hunting for the one Rei Kawakubo put out; we'll come to that story shortly. Over the past year, in fact, a number of tech-based lifestyle companies have started making magazines.

In November 2014, four years after it was founded, the rental platform Airbnb launched *Pineapple*, a 128-page magazine. The first issue covered three cities, London, Seoul and San Francisco, with plenty on food, art, culture and fashion.

In March this year, Uber launched Momentum, an in-house publication for drivers, with items such as "tricks for exercising while driving" and "the best local restaurants." It helps drivers and helps them get along better with passengers. Six months later, Uber announced on its official blog that it would launch its first magazine for passengers in New York, Arriving Now. The first issue takes New York Fashion Week as its theme and covers popular sights, shops around the city and more.

![Airbnb's Pineapple magazine](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703152016IS6weaRblKpqWZXH.jpg-w600)Airbnb's *Pineapple*

Airbnb and Uber, today's best-known sharing-economy companies, are valued at US$25.5 billion and more than US$50 billion respectively. Airbnb has more than 35 million users; Uber carries over a million people a day in more than 300 cities worldwide.

Airbnb sent the first 18,000 copies to hosts in the 3,400 cities across 190 countries where it operates, and at the same time released a small limited edition sold in bookstores, newsstands and boutiques. "Traveling with Airbnb isn't just about sightseeing and spending; it's more about relationships and community. Through the magazine, we hope travelers will feel a sense of belonging and have an unforgettable trip," Airbnb CEO Jonathan Mildenhall said at the launch. And the publications Uber aims at different groups of people no doubt carry its values along with the information.

So we see more and more companies like Uber and Airbnb trying their hand at publishing. The Taiwanese creative brand Mogu Shoutie has published a magazine of the same name for more than ten years, focused on the aesthetics of daily life. The fresh-food e-commerce site Benlai Life launched its own magazine in November 2014, about lifestyle and the stories behind food.

These magazines may well show fancier lives and experiences. That is their most direct pull on consumers: nobody turns down good content. For the companies, though, it is essentially brand marketing through content.

Whether it is Airbnb, Uber, Mogu Shoutie or Benlai Life, what they publish is all about lifestyle. More precisely, they want to shape your lifestyle. Only once you accept the brand's values and choose the lifestyle it promotes can it "tame" you into a more loyal customer.

This is an entirely different business logic from that of traditional magazines. A traditional magazine lives on more readers, which give it more clout to attract advertisers. These companies would also like more readers, but circulation is not what they care about; the reputation a magazine brings the brand matters more. Now do you see why they dare to be so edgy and bold?

Now we can talk about Rei Kawakubo. As early as the early 1990s, the Japanese designer published a magazine named after the "sixth sense": Six Magazine. It was filled with photography, with text taking up only a small part. Anyone who has seen her brand's print ads knows how unconventionally it defines "beauty." It genuinely breaks through tradition, convention and taboo, and sets out to explore the limits of the human form, color and ideas. That is true of its print ads, and just as true of its magazine.

![Rei Kawakubo's Six Magazine](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031520162jy38OPVxB5JHdQU.jpg-w600)Rei Kawakubo's *Six Magazine*

The online luxury retailer NET-A-PORTER and its men's luxury site MR PORTER take a different route. They are e-commerce businesses, and they want to be practical.

In that sense, their two digital publications, The EDIT and The Journal, are worth recommending (there is also a print title, THE MR PORTER POST, which is very good too). The line between fashion magazines and fashion brands was always blurry, and there is nothing wrong with a what-you-see-is-what-you-get feel. Personally, I find the men's title more captivating. It asks how the ideal man should be defined and what a so-called elegant lifestyle really is. In depth, it holds its own against any men's fashion magazine.

![PORTER, NET-A-PORTER's print magazine](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703152017vr17qPiTXVt5OexC.jpg-w600)PORTER, the print magazine NET-A-PORTER launched separately

![The Journal, Mr Porter's digital magazine](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703152017ZmyMCfDp6LUnBYuH.jpg-w600)The Journal, Mr Porter's digital magazine

![THE MR PORTER POST](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703152018lAFTL6HbwRyG0z98.jpg-w600)THE **MR PORTER** POST

As early as October 2012, Econsultancy, a digital marketing and e-commerce consultancy, published a report finding that 92% of brands and 71% of ad agencies had drawn up, or begun drawing up, a clear content marketing strategy. More and more companies want to use content marketing to promote their own importance.

At this point, "having an attitude" is no longer just a way to look cool; it is a condition of survival. What you say must have an attitude, and how it looks even more so. Otherwise, how could you call it a magazine?

When COLORS launched, people called it something special in what was then the MTV era. A good magazine relies on its physical quality and makes people want to keep it. The content is what earns it a place in their memory.

COLORS' three co-founders were an outstanding photographer, a designer and an editor, and before joining the magazine Tibor Kalman also owned a design firm, M&Co. In later issues they brought in different editors to collaborate. For issue 70, a special on the city of Beijing, COLORS brought in *New Vision*'s founders, Peng Yangjun and Chen Jiaojiao, as creative directors.

![Cover of COLORS issue 70, a special on Beijing](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703152018yFfiQga7HoJmbVOj.jpg-w600)COLORS issue 70, a special on the city of Beijing

Airbnb hired Alex Tieghi Walker, formerly an editor at Nowness, LVMH's fashion and arts site, as editor-in-chief of *Pineapple*; he picks freelance writers to fill out the magazine. Lucy Yeomans, who has run publications across NET-A-PORTER.com's platforms since 2012, spent 11 years at the British edition of *Harper's Bazaar*.

When Yeomans left *Harper's Bazaar* in 2012, her British readership for the first half of the year was 120,000. In her new job at NET-A-PORTER.com, she reaches more than 5 million readers a month. That same year, single-copy magazine sales in the US fell 9.5% to 26.7 million, almost half the figure of ten years earlier.

You will naturally think of the decline of print. A common question goes: if even the big-name magazines and newspapers are failing, who is going to read this arty stuff?

It is a question of mindset. Paper used to be merely a vehicle for content. Now that the internet has solved the problem of spreading information efficiently, paper's role in spreading it will naturally shrink. In other words, whatever gets printed now has to be genuinely good. A magazine engages every sense but taste, and pixels can hardly match the fine, subtle texture of print. If you are pessimistic about print, it may well be because you have never seen a truly valuable magazine or newspaper.

On this point, the internet has done something rather good: it has washed away, bit by bit, the outdated and half-hearted print publications. Truly valuable content will find all sorts of suitable vehicles: the internet, paper, perhaps something else entirely.

If even you think what you make isn't cool enough, what right do you have to complain when you're weeded out?
